extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 (MPEP §§2144–2144.08): tests, factors, and case-law examples for determining whether claimed subject matter is obvious over the prior art, including special topics (ranges, species/genus, purity, equivalence, rearrangement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere scaling up of a prior art process
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere scaling up of a prior art process capable of being scaled up does not establish patentability in a claim to an old process so scaled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite case law (e.g., 531 F.2d at 1053). Scaling up without new or unexpected results is not a patentable distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of relative dimensions without different performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only difference between the prior art and the claims is a recitation of relative dimensions and a device having the claimed relative dimensions would not perform differently, the claimed device is not patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Gardner v. TEC Systems, Inc.; structural changes must produce different function or result to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reordering of process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the order of prior art process steps is prima facie obvious absent new or unexpected results produced by the reordered steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Rubin and In re Burhans/In re Gibson: selection of any order of performing process steps is prima facie obvious unless there are new/unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making portable
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact that a claimed device is portable or movable is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over an otherwise old device unless there are new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Lindberg (portable/movable feature alone insufficient). Assess whether portability yields unexpected advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making integral (one-piece construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming that parts are made integral (one-piece) instead of multiple parts is not necessarily patentable; one-piece construction may be 'merely a matter of obvious engineering choice' unless it produces new/unexpected results that are contrary to prior art expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cases: In re Larson (one-piece not patentable) vs. Schenck v. Nortron (one-piece eliminated need for damping and produced unexpected insight). Evaluate whether the integral construction changes function or overcomes art-recognized problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making separable (removable parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a part manually removable (separable) where prior art had a press-fit or non-removable version is obvious if it would be an obvious expedient to obtain access or benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dulberg: if access or other desire exists, making a cap removable is obvious. Consider whether prior art provided motivation for removability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making adjustable
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting adjustable mechanisms (e.g., universal joint for single pivot) where the art recognizes a need for adjustment is not a patentable advance and is prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Stevens: where adjustability is needed and art recognizes that need, ordinary substitutions to provide adjustment are routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making continuous vs batch
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing a batch process to continuous operation is prima facie obvious where the prior art process differs only in requiring the addition/operation to be continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dilnot: claimed continuous operation would have been obvious in light of batch prior art absent evidence of unexpected results from continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing movement or placement of parts (so the part moves with a different structure) is an obvious expedient unless it produces new/unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Gazda: mere reversal that does not modify operation is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication of parts has no patentable significance unless it produces a new and unexpected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Harza: absence of plurality in reference does not render claimed duplication patentable unless novel results arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rearranging parts of a reference device is not by itself sufficient to support obviousness; the prior art must provide a motivation or reason for the worker in the art to make the necessary changes without benefit of the applicant’s specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Japikse and In re Kuhle: show motivation in the prior art; Ex parte Chicago Rawhide Mfg. Co. emphasizes the need for prior-art motivation to rearrange parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying an old product
rubrics_metrics.description: Purer forms of known products may be patentable, but mere purity by itself does not render the product unobvious; purified materials are novel vis-à-vis impure materials, but unobviousness depends on other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the claimed compound/composition has the same utility as related prior-art materials and whether the prior art suggests the particular form/structure or methods of obtaining it. See In re Bergstrom, In re Cofer, Ex parte Gray, Ex parte Stern. Applicant bears burden to show unexpected properties or that prior art did not provide methods to obtain the purified form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of overlapping or close ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are close enough that one skilled in the art would expect similar properties may also be prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Wertheim, In re Woodruff, In re Geisler, Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner. Consider whether prior-art numeric language (e.g., 'about') creates an overlap. If prior art range is extremely broad (genus-like), additional analysis may be required (see In re Baird, In re Jones). Multiple references can collectively disclose a 'range.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization within prior art conditions / routine experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering optimum or workable concentrations, temperatures, or other parameters within general prior-art conditions is not inventive; routine experimentation to find optimums does not support patentability absent evidence of criticality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Aller, In re Hoeschele, Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kulling, In re Geisler: show evidence of criticality (e.g., critical temperature or concentration) to overcome routine optimization presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only result-effective variables can be optimized to establish nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A parameter must be recognized as a result-effective variable (i.e., one that achieves a recognized result) before optimization of that parameter can be characterized as more than routine experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Antonie: if prior art did not recognize the parameter as result-effective, optimization might not be routine and could support nonobviousness. Evaluate whether prior art recognized the parameter's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal of prima facie obviousness for ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness based on overlapping ranges by showing criticality (unexpected results), by showing that the prior art teaches away, or by adducing secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, copying) with nexus to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Woodruff, In re Geisler, Iron Grip Barbell Co. v. USA Sports. Secondary considerations must have nexus and be supported by evidence; courts scrutinize licenses, copying, market absence, etc., when assessing such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining equivalents known for the same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is prima facie obvious to combine two compositions each taught by the prior art to be useful for the same purpose to form a third composition for that same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kerkhoven, In re Crockett, Ex parte Quadranti: when components are individually taught for a purpose, combination flows logically. Examiner should treat such combinations as prima facie obvious unless rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting equivalents known for the same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of one component by an art-recognized equivalent for the same purpose may support an obviousness rejection, but the equivalency must be recognized in the prior art and cannot be based solely on the applicant's disclosure or mere functional equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Ruff, Smith v. Hayashi, In re Fout: show evidence that the prior art recognizes the equivalency (e.g., both known photoconductors in the art) rather than relying on applicant's Markush grouping or after-the-fact functional equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of known material for suitability for an intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a known material from a list because it is suitable for a known intended use supports a prima facie obviousness determination; 'reading a list and selecting a known compound to meet known requirements is no more ingenious than selecting the last piece to put in the last opening in a jig-saw puzzle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., In re Leshin, Ryco v. Ag-Bag: selection based on suitability (e.g., solvent with particular vapor pressure) is prima facie obvious when prior art teaches the desired properties and lists suitable compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of species when prior art teaches a genus — avoid per se rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species, Office personnel should not apply per se rules; instead analyze whether the claimed species/subgenus would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill considering the totality of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Papesch, In re Brouwer, In re Ochiai, In re Baird, In re Deuel. The fact that a species falls within a prior-art genus is not by itself sufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a prima facie case of obviousness (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper obviousness analysis involves (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims; (C) determining the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluating any evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to applicant to come forward with rebuttal evidence/argument. See Graham v. John Deere and cases such as In re Bell, In re Rijckaert, In re Oetiker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the scope and content of the prior art (35 U.S.C. 102 and analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reference relied upon must qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and should be analogous art; Office personnel should make findings on structure, properties/utilities, predictability, and number of species encompassed when a genus is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2141.01(a), Ryko v. Nu-Star: evaluate prior art from viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill. Make explicit findings about the prior-art genus structure and disclosed species/subgenera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus and the claimed species/subgenus
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the closest disclosed species/subgenus in the prior art and compare it to the claimed species/subgenus; make explicit findings on similarities/differences including structure, chemical properties, and utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Stratoflex: focus on whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious. Examiners should compare structures and properties and document the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should determine the level of ordinary skill in the relevant art because it frames the obviousness inquiry and affects evaluation of motivation and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of skill level usually comes from the prior art references, but consider any additional evidence presented by applicant (Ryko v. Nu-Star, Uniroyal v. Rudkin-Wiley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species/subgenus
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering prior-art findings (scope/content, differences, skill level), determine whether it would have been obvious to make the claimed invention as a whole — i.e., to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on teachings in the prior art: (a) size of the genus; (b) express teachings that point to selection; (c) teachings of structural similarity; (d) predictability of the technology. Consider express suggestions to select or references that refer to one another (Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kemps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the size of the genus when evaluating species obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the prior art genus bears on whether a claimed species would have been envisioned by one skilled in the art, but size alone cannot support obviousness; the totality of circumstances matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, highly constrained genera (e.g., only 20 compounds with few variations) may render species obvious (In re Petering, In re Schaumann); broad genera may not. Evaluate number of species, variability, and other contextual factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider express teachings and structural similarity in motivating selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art expressly teaches a reason to select the claimed species/subgenus or discloses a 'typical', 'preferred', or 'optimum' species structurally similar to the claimed species, that may provide motivation to select the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural relationships (homologs, preferred species) often motivate selection because similar structures usually have similar properties (Dillon, Deuel). Point to explicit cross-reference between prior-art disclosures when present.
